a1-copula.title: The Noun-Class Copula: вуго / йиго / буго / руго
a1-copula.pattern: [subject, bare form] + вуго (masculine) / йиго (feminine) / буго (default/non-human) / руго (plural)
a1-copula.explanation: Avar's "to be"/"there is" doesn't have one fixed shape -- like its sister Northeast Caucasian languages, it changes to agree with the grammatical class of its subject. A masculine human subject takes вуго (Чи вуго -- "there is a man"), a feminine human subject takes йиго (Чӏужу йиго -- "there is a woman"), and most other subjects -- objects, animals, abstract things -- take буго (Лъим буго -- "there is water"). Plural subjects take руго (Нилъ руго -- "we are [here]").
a1-copula.fact: This в-/й-/б-/р- agreement pattern is one of the defining features of the Northeast Caucasian family Avar belongs to, and it doesn't stop at this one verb -- the same class markers reappear as prefixes across many other verbs, adjectives, and even some postpositions throughout the language. The masculine/feminine/default three-way split (вуго/йиго/буго) is well documented in academic descriptions; the plural form руго is corroborated independently but with a narrower confirmed example base so far, so treat it as attested-but-still-being-verified, the same caution applied to a comparable uncertain form early in this app's Chechen course.

a2-possession-dir.title: Possession: дир (my)
a2-possession-dir.pattern: дир (my) + [possessed noun, bare form] + copula (agreeing with the POSSESSED noun's class)
a2-possession-dir.explanation: Avar doesn't have a separate verb "to have" -- possession is expressed the same way existence is, with the copula from the previous lesson (вуго/йиго/буго). The possessor goes first as дир ("my", the genitive form of дун "I"), then the possessed noun, then the copula -- and the copula agrees with the CLASS OF THE THING POSSESSED, not with "I": Дир вас вуго ("my son is [here]" / "I have a son") takes вуго because вас (son) is masculine, while Дир яс йиго takes йиго because яс (daughter) is feminine.
a2-possession-dir.fact: This possessor-in-genitive-plus-copula pattern is well documented in the academic literature on Avar (compare the classic textbook example "Ali's car is [there]" = "Ali has a car"). Only дир ("my") is used here -- the possessive forms for "your", "his/her", "our", and "their" haven't been confirmed from a reliable source yet, so they're deliberately left for a later round rather than guessed.

dialogue.en: I have a son. / My son is here.

b1-possession-dur.title: Possession: дур (your)
b1-possession-dur.pattern: дур (your, singular) + [possessed noun, bare form] + copula (agreeing with the POSSESSED noun's class)
b1-possession-dur.explanation: Just like дир ("my", from дун "I"), дур is the genitive/possessive form of мун ("you", singular) -- "your". It slots into the exact same possession frame from the previous lesson: possessor first, then the bare possessed noun, then the copula agreeing with what's possessed. Дур вас вуго ("your son is [here]") takes вуго because вас is masculine, exactly as дир вас вуго did.
b1-possession-dur.fact: Both дир and дир's counterpart дур appear side by side in a real academic example sentence ("my shirt is different from yours"), which is what confirms дур here -- that source sentence uses a more complex comparative construction ("than yours") that isn't reused in this lesson, since it needs additional case morphology that hasn't been independently confirmed yet for other nouns. Possessive forms for "his/her", "our", and "their" are still unconfirmed and deliberately left for a later round.
